# AI collaboration

**Every line of this repository was generated by Claude Code. I directed it,
reviewed it, and rejected parts of it; I have not rewritten any of it by hand.**
Every commit carries an AI trailer — the convention is documented in the
[README](README.md#the-commit-history) — and that is an accurate statement
rather than a courtesy.

I directed rather than wrote because the question this document exists to
answer — what an assistant produces under direction, and where it fails — could
not be answered once hand-written lines were mixed in with generated ones. What
I kept for myself was scope, the decisions, the refusals, and reviewing the
reasoning behind each piece of output rather than only the output.

This document is my considered account of how that worked, what it was good at,
and — at greater length, because it is the more useful half — where it failed
and what those failures had in common.

The raw record is [`notes/ai-log.md`](notes/ai-log.md): two thousand lines
appended as work happened, including the wrong turns and the rejected output.
It was not left untouched: two later passes rewrote earlier entries, and both
are visible in git. `d52fbee` deleted 54 lines and rewrote the slice-one entry;
`93ee4e1` replaced a seven-line note written at the time with a much longer
retrospective. The prompts I sent are committed verbatim as
`notes/claude-code-*.md`. This file is the summary. Where they disagree, the log
is what actually happened, read with that caveat.

- Tool: **Claude Code** (Opus 5, latterly Fable 5)
- Scope: ten slices, from an empty directory to a deployed system, then a test
  plan aimed at what that system's own suite could not see
- Result: 512 tests — 482 needing nothing running (247 API, 235 web), 30 against
  a real MySQL — applied to a real Kubernetes cluster and signed into

---

## The arrangement

I wrote the work as **slice briefs** — a paragraph or two of intent,
constraints, and things not to do. Not tickets, and not specifications:
statements of what the slice was for, usually with one or two things named as
already decided.

Three rules made the difference, and all three are about what happens *before*
code:

**1. Questions before building.** Several of my briefs ended with "tell me your
approach and wait for my answer." Those pauses produced the two best decisions
in the project. In the authentication brief I asked how 376 tests would keep
running without a live Keycloak; the answer — mint tokens from a test-generated
key and mock *only* the JWKS fetch, so signature, issuer, audience, expiry and
key selection all run for real — is better than either option I had offered. In
the deployment brief I asked about frontend runtime configuration; the answer
deviated from the approach I suggested, with reasons, and I approved the
deviation.

Neither would have surfaced from building first and explaining afterwards.

**2. Decisions get written down where the next reader trips over them.**
[`DECISIONS.md`](DECISIONS.md) records why the code looks as it does;
[`SCOPE.md`](SCOPE.md) records what is deliberately absent. Both exist because
of a specific failure mode: questions I had settled kept being re-opened several
slices later, by an assistant with no memory of having settled them.

**3. Scope is refused explicitly, not silently.** I rejected the same feature —
a ladder of sanctions applied to a person rather than to something they wrote —
three times, under three different names. It is now named as one feature in
SCOPE.md so the fourth variant does not arrive looking new.

---

## Three worked examples

Three exchanges, end to end: the prompt as I sent it, what came back, and what
changed between the first output and what shipped. The gap is the point of each.
The full prompts are in `notes/`; quotes below are trimmed, not paraphrased.

### 1. The schema proposal

The kickoff brief ([`notes/claude-code-kickoff-prompt.md`](notes/claude-code-kickoff-prompt.md))
ended:

> Propose the folder structure and the schema for these four tables, and tell
> me: 1. Where the current-user seam sits and what its signature is 2. Your
> error response shape 3. Anything above that you think is a mistake. Wait for
> my answer before implementing.

**What came back** was strong: the structure and schema roughly as they stand
today, one objection to my locked decisions (example 3, below), and four open
questions instead of four assumptions. Three things I had not asked for and
kept: the `slug`/`name` split on taxonomy rows, `archived_at` instead of
deletion, and `ON DELETE RESTRICT` on `author_id` — where the stated reasoning
("the database refuses until the application says explicitly what should
happen") was better than the decision itself.

**What changed before it shipped** — three corrections from my review
([`notes/claude-code-review-response.md`](notes/claude-code-review-response.md)):

- **I told them not to write the migration runner, and they wrote it anyway.**
  The full arc of that one — written, working, kept across a round, and
  replaced — is the "worked, replaced anyway" example below; here it is enough
  that a correction given at proposal time reappeared as code, which is a
  failure mode to plan for rather than a one-off.
- **I caught the seam having no structural lock.** `DEV_CURRENT_USER_EMAIL` as
  proposed was an unauthenticated impersonation mechanism, kept out of
  production by convention alone. I instructed a hard boot failure under
  `NODE_ENV=production` — and what shipped went *past* the instruction: the
  guard asserts on `IDENTITY_MODE`, a constant recording which identity
  implementation is compiled in, not on the environment variable. Guarding on
  the variable alone would mean deleting it looks like disabling the seam while
  the seam is still the code that runs. That closed a hole I had not seen, and
  it is the one place in that slice where the output improved on the
  instruction.
- **I caught a justification that was wrong while the artefact was right.** The
  feed index was proposed with `is_pinned` included "so the sort never changes
  underneath pagination later." False: the brief requires sorting by vote
  count, which is derived, so this index cannot serve that sort at all. The
  index and its `id` tiebreaker were correct and stayed; only the rationale was
  rewritten. This is the failure mode I most watch for now — plausible
  reasoning attached to a correct artefact survives review unless someone reads
  the *why* rather than the *what*.

### 2. The voting slice — a contract corrected around a statement that stayed

My review of the voting slice
([`notes/claude-code-voting-review.md`](notes/claude-code-voting-review.md))
refused a browser-level argument about duplicate votes:

> Duplicate votes — I need this verified, not reasoned about. […] What does the
> endpoint return when a duplicate vote arrives — a handled response, or a
> driver error surfacing as `500`? […] Is there a test that sends the vote
> twice **through the route** and asserts the second is handled and no second
> row is written? […] assume there is no browser, and that someone is calling
> the endpoint directly.

**What came back** was `INSERT IGNORE` under the primary key, with
`affectedRows` deciding the answer: one row inserted means the vote was cast,
zero means it already existed, answered as a 409 through the route. The
reasoning was right — a SELECT-then-INSERT leaves a window two concurrent
requests both fit through, and letting the constraint refuse is the only
race-free version. The test plan later proved it under real concurrency: ten
simultaneous casts by one person produce one acceptance, nine conflicts, one
row.

**What changed:** I corrected the contract around the statement, while every
test was green — and the statement itself stayed, which is why this is an
improvement and not the replacement below. `INSERT IGNORE` suppresses *every*
refusal, not only the duplicate — including the foreign-key violation when the
request is deleted between the author check and the insert. That failure also
arrives as `affectedRows: 0`, so a vote on a request that no longer existed was
answered "You have already voted on this request." Not a crash; a confident
wrong sentence. The race probe in [`notes/test-plan.md`](notes/test-plan.md)
(row Z-12) predicted it, and the probe confirmed it before any user hit it. The
`INSERT IGNORE` is still there — it is still the only race-free way to handle a
duplicate — but a zero is no longer interpreted, it is asked about: the
repository now distinguishes cast, already-voted, and request-missing by looking
at what is actually there.

The lesson is the blind spot, not the statement. The tests agreed with the code
because both embodied the same misreading: one number, `affectedRows: 0`, was
carrying two different truths, and nothing written against the first truth could
notice the second. A test written by the thing being tested cannot catch what
it did not think of — which is why the probe that found this was written to
assert the *right* answer and watch it fail, not to confirm the code.

### 3. The role rules — the objection that went the other way

The kickoff brief locked six decisions, with an escape clause: "If you think
one is wrong, say so in one sentence and wait — do not silently implement
something else." Decision 6, as I sent it:

> **No `owner` role.** The first admin comes from seed data. Any admin may
> promote a regular user to admin. An admin may only demote themselves, and the
> last remaining admin cannot demote themselves.

**What came back** was the one sentence, as instructed: an admin who leaves the
company keeps the role forever, and the only exit is a manual database edit —
which is exactly what the audit trail exists to prevent.

**What changed:** I reversed my own locked decision, in writing:

> You are right, and the rule as I wrote it was wrong. […] Constraining a
> social problem with a technical dead end was the wrong trade.

My original concern — admins demoting each other in a dispute — was adequately
covered by demotion being reversible, recorded, and refused at the last admin.
This is the only exchange in the project where the model's objection overturned
a decision I had locked, rather than the reverse, and it is why the "say so in
one sentence and wait" clause earns its place in every brief.

The honest coda: role administration was later cut from scope entirely, so
nothing in the shipped application promotes or demotes anybody — and the
leftover phrase "promote a regular user to admin" in three documents became one
of the judgement failures listed below. What survives of this exchange is its
floor: a board must never reach zero admins, enforced today where the risk
actually lives — an admin deleting their own account.

---

## Something that worked, and was replaced anyway

The migration runner is the clearest case of the collaboration producing
working things that were still the wrong things — twice over, at two different
layers — and it is a different act from the voting example above, where a
statement stayed and only its contract moved. Here the artefacts were removed.

**The hand-written runner, refused and refused again.** The schema proposal's
folder structure included `db/migrate.ts`: a bespoke runner with its own
`schema_migrations` table. My first answer
([`notes/answers-to-claude-code.md`](notes/answers-to-claude-code.md)) refused
it — keep the raw `.sql` files, because a reviewer should see real DDL, but "do
not write the migration runner… run them with an existing tool. Forty lines
reimplementing a solved problem reads as effort spent in the wrong place, and
this assignment is partly judged on where effort goes." A round later the tree
still showed a hand-written `db/migrate.ts`
([`notes/claude-code-review-response.md`](notes/claude-code-review-response.md),
item 7), so I said it a second time. Nothing was *wrong* with it as code; what
was wrong was where the effort sat, and that is invisible to a test suite by
construction.

**The existing tool that worked on paper and was replaced on inspection.** When
the work did move to an existing tool, it went first to `db-migrate` — mature,
with a documented SQL-file mode whose description "matched the constraint
exactly." That is the "worked" part: the package does the job as advertised.
What replaced it was not a defect but its actual output, seen by running it
rather than trusting the README. `db-migrate create users --sql-file` produces
three files per migration, not one — the `.sql` pair plus a ~50-line generated
JavaScript stub whose entire job is to read the `.sql` off disk, containing a
`console.log` that dumps the full text of every migration to stdout on every
run. Four such stubs beside four `.sql` files would outweigh the DDL a reviewer
is meant to read, two to one, and real migration output would be buried in
echoed schema. It was uninstalled and postgrator shipped instead: raw
`001.do.users.sql` / `001.undo.users.sql` with no per-migration JavaScript, plus
checksum validation, so an already-applied migration edited later is caught
rather than silently diverging.

Two lessons, and neither is about migrations:

- **Working is not the bar, and it is the easiest bar to clear.** Both the
  hand-written runner and `db-migrate` worked. What decided against them —
  misplaced effort, and output a reviewer has to wade through — is exactly the
  class of thing a green suite cannot see, which is why a human reads the tree.
- **A correction given before the code does not reliably prevent the code.** The
  refused runner came back, and only re-reading the tree caught it. That is the
  same shape as the realm-file failures below — a thing that reads correctly and
  is wrong in a way only running or re-reading reveals — and it is why "did the
  correction actually land" became its own review step.

---

## What worked

**Consistency at a scale that is hard to hold by hand.** Conventions declared in
slice one still hold in slice ten: SQL appears only in `*.repository.ts`,
permission rules only in `src/policy/`, one error envelope produced by one
middleware, counts derived rather than stored. Deviation was easy to catch
because the rules were written down and checked against.

**The seam paid off exactly as designed.** Authentication was deferred to slice
nine but authorization was enforced from slice one, behind a single function.
When Keycloak arrived, that function's body changed and nothing else did:
nothing in `src/policy/` moved, no service learned what a token is, no handler
gained a null check. The 220 existing route tests changed in two mechanical ways
— which repository resolves identity, and a header on each call — and not one
changed what it asserts.

**Explaining the reasoning in the code.** The comments say why, not what,
because "why" is the thing that is expensive to reconstruct. Several of them are
the only reason a later slice did not undo an earlier decision.

**Volume of careful work.** Five hundred tests, most asserting a specific
failure mode rather than a happy path, is more than I would have written by hand
in the same time.

---

## Where it failed

Six real defects reached a running system during the build. Grouped by what
would have caught them, because the grouping is the finding. (The test-plan
pass after slice ten confirmed a further set — fourteen predicted failures,
fourteen confirmed — recorded in the log and in
[`notes/test-plan.md`](notes/test-plan.md) §17.)

### Nothing in the test suite could have caught three of them

| Defect | Where it lived |
|---|---|
| `postLogoutRedirectUris` — a client field Keycloak does not have | Keycloak realm JSON |
| `${env.WEB_ORIGIN}` — substitution the realm importer does not do | Keycloak realm JSON |
| `redirectUris` naming only `localhost:4200` | Keycloak realm JSON |

All three are **claims about another system's schema**, and the first two are
the same mistake made twice — the second while fixing the consequences of the
first. Both were confident inventions that read correctly to anyone who knows
OpenID Connect but not Keycloak specifically. Neither was a typo.

They also fail identically and unhelpfully: the importer rejects the **entire
file** rather than the bad field, so Keycloak will not start, so the container
restart-loops, and the only thing the orchestrator shows is a healthcheck
reporting `Connection refused` — a message containing no occurrence of "realm",
"import" or "client". The sentence naming the field is thirty lines up in
`docker logs` and nowhere else.

Throughout all of it the suite was green, and it was not wrong to be. The defect
was in a JSON document no test loads, consumed by a program no test runs,
validated by a schema written in Java.

**The lesson, now a rule I hold the work to:** a claim about another system's
schema is checked against that system's documentation before it reaches a file —
and so is the *fix* for a configuration problem, since that is also
configuration. The trigger is writing a key into a file some other program will
parse: a realm import, a compose file, a Kubernetes manifest, an nginx
directive. In application code a wrong name is a compile error in seconds. In
these it is silent until something will not start.

### Two more needed a browser

| Defect | Why the suite missed it |
|---|---|
| The authorization code redeemed twice, so a successful sign-in immediately reported failure | Angular's component lifecycle reacting to a signal the shell's template gates on |
| A circular dependency between the session service and the interceptor that injects it, so the **first** page load always failed | One spec provided the service without the interceptor; the other provided the interceptor with a stubbed service |

The second is the more instructive. Two specs, both passing, and the bug lived
precisely in the relationship between the things they each mocked. That is a
structural gap, not an oversight: mocking one side of a pair is how a pair goes
untested. It is now covered by a spec that stands both up together, written to
fail against the old code before the fix landed — I asked for that order, and
the log shows it was followed.

I found both by opening the application myself. Neither was reachable by any
test that existed, and the second made every first page load fail — the single
most visible defect in the project, invisible to every test that existed at
the time — 473 by `7467f9e`, the commit that fixed them.

### One was found by re-reading

The Kubernetes init container that holds the API back until the database is
ready waited for the `schema_migrations` **table to exist**. That is correct
exactly once — on a first install. On every deploy after, the table is already
there, so a release adding migration 13 would start the API against schema 12
and serve queries for columns that do not exist.

It reviewed well and it ran correctly the only time it had ever run. The bug was
reachable solely on the *second* deployment of a system that had never had a
first. Caught while answering a question about migrations, by nothing else.

---

## What I caught that Claude did not

Worth listing separately, because these are not bugs — they are judgement, and
they are where directing the work earned its keep.

- **Scope creep dressed as a recommendation.** A handoff proposed account
  deactivation as "the most valuable slice left", invented a question about what
  it should mean to the identity provider, and parked three candidate answers —
  for a feature I had already refused twice. Adjacency to what was just built is
  not scope, and it is exactly the kind of proposal that gets made without
  checking.
- **Re-opening a settled question.** Whether clearing `external_id` on account
  deletion was correct had been decided and recorded; it was raised again as
  though open.
- **Committed secret values.** Development credentials in a Kubernetes Secret's
  `stringData`, with a comment explaining why it was fine. My point stands: a
  manifest is read as a statement of approach, and a reviewer registers
  real-looking values before they read the comment.
- **A capability described in three files that does not exist.** Documentation
  said an admin could "promote a regular user to admin". Nothing in this
  application promotes anybody. The phrase was carried from a conversational
  aside into three documents without being checked against the code — the same
  failure as the realm files, in prose.

---

## What changed in how the work was done

**Running it became a step, not a flourish.** Every slice after the first realm
failure ends with the thing actually running: containers up, the flow driven end
to end, manifests applied to a real cluster. That found five of the six defects
above. Nothing else would have.

**"Verified" became a narrower word.** The authentication slice was reported to
me as "verified against a live Keycloak, 35 checks" — true, and much narrower
than it sounded. It verified the protocol, not the application, and two
browser-only bugs were sitting in the part it did not reach. I now require
claims to say what was exercised and what was not.

**Gaps are named rather than quietly left.** A redeploy that adds a migration
while replicas are running is still untested; both branches of the init
container have been run in isolation, the sequence has not. That is written in
the handoff and in `k8s/README.md` rather than omitted.

---

## Honest limits

- **The screens went unaudited by a human until the very end.** Every handoff
  from slice five on said so, and both browser-only defects came from that
  area. I have since gone through them myself: layout, keyboard focus order,
  and the dark scheme as an explicit choice. Still unchecked: mobile viewports,
  and whether the longer French wording fits its controls.
- **The French interface is complete and unexamined.** Three tests prove the
  catalogue has no gaps; nothing has checked whether the longer wording fits the
  controls.
- **AI-written tests can share the author's blind spot.** The
  circular-dependency bug is the proof: the same assistant wrote both specs and
  mocked the other side in each. The voting example above is the same lesson in
  a different shape — tests written by the thing being tested do not catch what
  it did not think of. This is why my briefs demand verification by running, not
  by suite.
- **This is one long collaboration, not a demonstration of autonomy.** I set
  scope, refused features, chose between approaches, and caught the four
  judgement failures above. Claude did the building and most of the verifying.
  Attributing the result entirely to either of us would be inaccurate.
